articles.title: Ms Rachel calls Gaza journalist ‘friend’ in resurfaced clip after he admits hiding Oct 7 hostage footage
articles.summary: Children's YouTube star Ms. Rachel faces scrutiny after a resurfaced video shows her calling Motaz Azaiza her "friend" amid his Oct. 7 revelations.
articles.body: Children's YouTube star Ms. Rachel faced renewed scrutiny on Sunday after a 2025 video of her calling Palestinian photojournalist Motaz Azaiza her "friend," resurfaced, days after Azaiza admitted he deliberately withheld footage of Israeli hostages being beaten by a crowd in Gaza on Oct. 7, 2023. The short video appears to show Ms. Rachel, whose real name is Rachel Griffin Accurso, introducing Azaiza to her young audience while teaching the letter "M." "Hi, yes, it’s M, for my friend, Motaz. Yay! Bye!" Accurso said. MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER The video was originally shared on Instagram and later removed, according to reporting from July 2025. Azaiza, who amassed millions of social media followers documenting the war in Gaza, appeared briefly in the clip and greeted Ms. Rachel. The video also took on new significance after Azaiza described earlier this month what he witnessed during the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attack in an extensive interview with journalist Ahmed al-Biqawi on the Arabic-language "Taqarrab" podcast. Azaiza said he followed a vehicle carrying Israeli captives and filmed as members of a crowd assaulted them. Azaiza said he didn't publish the video, however, as he feared it could put the Palestinians involved at risk. "I saw the vehicle of the Al-Qassam Brigades, and there were Israeli captives there," Azaiza said. "People got out, watched, beat them, hit them, and I followed them and filmed. But I did not publish those videos. Why? Because I did not want to ruin the lives of the people who were filmed." MS RACHEL POSTS SUPPORT FOR HIJAB-WEARING KINDERGARTNERS AFTER TRUMP POST Azaiza said he withheld the footage because he believed Israeli authorities could use it to identify the Palestinians appearing in the videos. "I understood that Israel would use those videos to identify every person who was there and eliminate them," Azaiza said. "I did not want to be responsible, even indirectly, for the deaths of those people in exchange for a few likes and views online." NEW YORK TIMES ISSUES CORRECTION, DELETES LINE QUESTIONING IF ISRAELIS WERE VICTIMS OF OCT 7 TERROR ATTACK Azaiza also criticized Hamas and described the restrictions faced by journalists working inside Gaza. He said photographers learned to lower their cameras when Palestinians criticized Hamas because showing such dissent could lead to retaliation. Despite describing himself as a supporter of armed Palestinian resistance, Azaiza said Hamas' actions had failed to protect Palestinians living in Gaza. "I support armed resistance, but one that brings results, or at least gives me the feeling that my life is valuable in the eyes of the resistance," Azaiza said. "Why should a Palestinian be cheap in the eyes of Palestinians themselves? You are making people hate the resistance with your own hands." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Azaiza's profile rose dramatically after the war began. Time named him to its 2024 list of the world's 100 most influential people for his photographs documenting Gaza. Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, told Fox News Digital that Azaiza’s disclosure raised questions about his journalistic judgment and his decision to withhold the footage. "After years spent claiming to share what was happening in Gaza ‘unfiltered,’ Azaiza revealed that he hid footage — not, per journalistic norms, to protect victims from further harm, but because he didn't want Israel to arrest the perpetrators. Innocent civilians had been kidnapped, already sexually abused, and his concern was with the people that beat them and rejoiced at Hamas' crimes. That speaks volumes about his journalism and his moral character," Menken said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Accurso, meanwhile, has become increasingly outspoken about Gaza. Last week, she accused celebrities and other public figures who had remained silent about Palestinian children of applying a racial double standard. "They probably would say something if these kids were White and from a different place," Accurso said. "Please stop being racist and risk something." Elizabeth Barcohana, the California Republican Party’s Jewish engagement chair, told Fox News Digital that she believed Accurso’s Gaza advocacy was spreading misleading information to her large audience. "Ms. Rachel is essentially sanitizing terrorism with false and misleading information to emotionally manipulate her very impressionable following and those around her in her industry," Barcohana said. Fox News Digital reached out to Ms. Rachel for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title: France’s Macron and Canada’s Carney announce plans to build stronger ties
articles.summary: Announcement comes as Canada seeks a closer relationship with the EU amid a trade war with the US.
articles.body:
Canada and France will pursue cooperation on energy, defence, space and other sectors, in what their leaders say is a reflection of shared values between the two countries.

The announcement was made on Sunday during a joint media conference by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron on the island archipelago of Saint Pierre and Miquelon in the North Atlantic.

The French territory is only about 25km (15.5 miles) from Newfoundland in Canada. Macron said it is a reflection of the historic closeness between the two countries, who “see the present from the same angle”.

Parts of Canada were once French colonies and French is still one of Canada’s two official languages, along with English.

“We both believe in democracy, in the rule of law, in the respect of international law, in the respect of free and fair commerce and trade,” Macron said alongside Carney. “That is why we support this future alliance, that you named as an associate member of the EU.”

Carney said both countries see eye to eye on protecting sovereignty, and that this meant going beyond “being able to feed, fuel and defend ourselves” to being able to secure access to AI, space, semiconductors, critical minerals and clean energy. Carney said the time had come to strengthen bonds between Canada, France and the European Union based on their “shared values”.

The remarks came as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States amid the escalating trade dispute between the neighbours and instead move closer to the EU.

Carney has said Canada seeks a “unique alliance” with the economic and political bloc, which would fall short of being a full member state. Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member.”

Canadian and European leaders have openly said they want to forge closer bonds to distance themselves from the United States and the political direction it seems to be going.

“I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners,” Carney said in a speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday. “We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

United States President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to annex Canada and make it the “51st state”. He has also called for Greenland to be taken away from Denmark and made a part of the US. But this week, he said he was happy with an agreement that he claimed would give Washington “permanent control” over the island, which largely enjoys self-rule but is still a part of Denmark. Both Greenland and Denmark said after the agreement was announced that any deal with the US would not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty.

Trump has called Ottawa’s attempt to move closer to the EU “laughable” and said he would have to study exactly what membership would mean. If it did not satisfy him, Trump said it could be seen as a “hostile act”.

“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs,” Trump said. He also suggested that the US could stop trading with Europe “on many things”.

Canada and the US have been locked in a trade war after failing to reach an agreement. The Trump administration imposed up to 50 percent tariffs on nearly $20bn worth of Canadian products, including machinery, textiles and even hockey sticks. Canada imposed retaliatory measures and the impasse continues.

articles.summary: Plainfield police seized 650 rolls of toilet paper in "Operation Clean Sweep" after masked groups targeted homes near Plainfield North High School.
articles.body: After warning students not to let homecoming pranks cross the line, an Illinois police department found itself staring down one very unusual haul. Plainfield police intercepted a massive toilet paper stash allegedly headed for neighborhood homes after reports of masked groups targeting the area near Plainfield North High School. "And yes… 650 rolls. We counted," police said. Police displayed the haul under an "Operation Clean Sweep" banner and jokingly gave it an estimated "street value" of $1,708.66 after two nights of escalating complaints from the surrounding community. TRENDING 'SENIOR ASSASSIN' GAME DRAWS STARK WARNINGS FROM POLICE NATIONWIDE: 'DANGEROUS MISUNDERSTANDINGS' "Homecoming is not a free pass to damage someone else's property or disrupt their quality of life," the department wrote on Facebook. FLORIDA POLICE DEPARTMENT GOES VIRAL WITH GENIUS STRATEGY TO CONNECT WITH COMMUNITY Officers received double-digit calls for service involving teens on both Monday and Tuesday during a two-hour period beginning shortly after 7 p.m. in the area surrounding the high school, according to police. Residents reported that homes and vehicles had been targeted with toilet paper, eggs, ketchup, detergent pods and other items. Police said groups of 20 to 25 people wearing hoodies and ski masks would "pull up" in several vehicles at the same time and "cause chaos." STUDENT CHARGED, WEAPON RECOVERED AFTER 3 TEENS TARGETED IN INCIDENT LINKED TO HIGH SCHOOL TRADITION: POLICE The targets were not limited to friends or classmates. Some of the homes belonged to families with small children or residents with no children at all, police said. "At this point, we are seeing property damage and significant cleanup, and residents are understandably frustrated," the department wrote. COPS HALT PLANNED 'TEEN TAKEOVER' AS OFFICIALS BRACE FOR A SUMMER SURGE IN CHAOS AND ARRESTS: POLICE CHIEF The department also made clear that the homecoming calls were pulling police attention from more serious incidents. Officers assisted firefighters at a structure fire, helped Illinois State Police, made a DUI arrest and responded to crashes, intoxicated people, violations of protection orders and a family experiencing a mental health crisis, according to the post. "In short, we DO have better things to do," police wrote. "So PLEASE, be respectful of your community and let us!" The department did not say where officers found the toilet paper, whether any arrests were made or whether charges had been filed in connection with the reported damage. "‘It was just a prank’ doesn’t erase the consequences," police warned in the earlier post. articles.title: Meet Sai Sri Valli Mogilineedi, the Mechanicsburg eighth-grader who designed a controlled-release antacid and became one of 30 US finalists competing for more than $100,000 in STEM awards
articles.summary: US News: An eighth-grader from Pennsylvania has been named one of the top 30 middle school researchers in the United States after developing a new way to deliv.
articles.body: An eighth-grader from Pennsylvania has been named one of the top 30 middle school researchers in the United States after developing a new way to deliver medicines used to treat Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD). Sai Sri Valli Mogilineedi, a student at Mountain View Middle School in Mechanicsburg, was named a national finalist in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge on 16 September 2026. The competition is organised by the non-profit Society for Science and is considered one of the leading US competitions for middle school students in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM).Mogilineedi’s project, titled "A Novel Controlled Release System for GERD Drugs Using Immobilization Techniques," looks at ways to improve how antacid medicines are released inside the body. Her research focuses on problems with common heartburn treatments by exploring controlled-release methods that could make the medicine work for longer. She will travel to Washington, DC, from 23 to 28 October for the competition's Finals Week. The 30 finalists were selected from 1,997 applicants across the country and will compete for more than $100,000 in educational awards.Developing longer-lasting heartburn treatmentMogilineedi’s research focuses on GERD, a long-term digestive condition in which stomach acid often flows back into the tube between the mouth and stomach. Common over-the-counter antacids can reduce stomach acid quickly, but their effects often do not last very long. This can mean that patients need to take several doses during the day. To address this problem, Mogilineedi used immobilization techniques to create a controlled-release system. The method is designed to release the active ingredients in antacid medicine slowly instead of releasing everything at once. Before reaching the national competition, Mogilineedi tested her idea at regional science competitions. According to records from the Capital Area Science and Engineering Fair (CASEF), her project received awards including the Penn State College of Medicine Award and the Love Award during regional judging.From local competitions to the national finalsMogilineedi’s path to the top 30 started at local science fairs. Society for Science says students must finish in the top 10 per cent of their local fairs to be nominated for the Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. Of nearly 2,000 students who entered nationally, a panel of scientists, engineers, and educators first selected the Top 300 Junior Innovators in September. The group was then reduced to 30 finalists representing 17 US states and Puerto Rico. Maya Ajmera, President and CEO of Society for Science and Executive Publisher of Science News, praised this year's finalists for focusing on real-world problems in an official statement. "Every year, our Thermo Fisher JIC finalists remind us of what's possible when curiosity meets courage — even in middle school," Ajmera said. "This year's Top 30 are already using science to tackle problems that matter to their communities and the world. I'm proud to welcome these 30 remarkable young scientists and engineers to Washington, D.C., this October."Team challenges and final awardsDuring Finals Week in Washington, DC, students will be judged on their individual research as well as their performance in team STEM challenges. Organisers say the group activities will test critical thinking, communication, and the ability to solve problems together. Every finalist will receive a $500 cash prize. articles.body: REJINAGAR (MURSHIDABAD): The second act of the Rejinagar bypoll drama unfolded on Sunday, with AJUP chief Humayun Kabir, who won the seat four-and-a-half months ago, announcing that he would not campaign for his son and party candidate Golam Nabi Azad, citing “hostility” from the administration.Hours later, he said his son, too, would stay away from electioneering.Kabir’s statements came a day after the flip-flop by Mamata All India Trinamool Congress candidate Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, who had said on Saturday morning that he would withdraw his nomination for the Oct 6 bypoll, only to retract his statement in the afternoon.“I have decided not to campaign,” Kabir said. “Whoever I meet is being arrested or threatened. My people can get killed, their people can get killed, too.”Later, he announced, “As per the party’s latest decision, our candidate, Golam Nabi Azad, will also stay away from campaigning. articles.title: Russia wraps up first wartime parliamentary election, Kremlin set to retain control
articles.summary: Europe News: Russia on Sunday wrapped up its first parliamentary election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with President Vladimir Putin's United .
articles.body: Russia on Sunday wrapped up its first parliamentary election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party widely expected to retain its overwhelming control of the State Duma.The three-day vote was held amid a crackdown on political dissent, with major anti-war opposition figures imprisoned, exiled or barred from the ballot. Turnout stood at 56.66 per cent when polls closed, according to Russia's Central Election Commission.About 111 million voters were eligible to cast ballots for the 450-seat lower house. Half the seats are contested through party lists and the rest through single-seat constituencies.The election also included voting in four Ukrainian regions claimed by Russia after the war began, as well as Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014. Ukraine condemned the voting in Russian-held territories and urged other countries not to recognise the results. The European Union called it a "blatant violation of international law."The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that openly criticised the war, was removed from the ballot by Russia's Supreme Court last month, although some of its candidates remained in constituency races.Yabloko and the Communist Party also reported that some of their observers were turned away from polling stations and alleged other violations, including ballot boxes being opened after being sealed and voters being denied paper ballots. The claims could not be independently verified.Russia did not invite observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. OSCE Parliamentary Assembly President Pere Joan Pons said the decision breached Russia's commitments as a member of the organisation.Electronic voting in Moscow also came under scrutiny. Election chief Ella Pamfilova said the system had been targeted by cyberattacks. Independent outlet SotaVision reported glitches in electronic registration systems, while Kremlin critic Leonid Volkov urged voters: "Demand a paper ballot!"The election's final day coincided with a major wave of Ukrainian drone attacks. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces shot down 1,110 Ukrainian drones across Russia, Crimea and the Black Sea. Moscow regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov said two people were killed and 20 wounded.Preliminary election results were expected within hours of voting ending in western Russia.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A New Jersey family has owned a 135-acre Christmas tree farm for 80 years; the preserved property, with an 1839 barn, 21 acres of cropland and a guest cottage, is now listed for $1.485 million
articles.summary: US News: A historic 135-acre Christmas tree farm in Warren County, New Jersey, has been listed for $1.485 million (£1.11 million) after being owned by the same.
articles.body: A historic 135-acre Christmas tree farm in Warren County, New Jersey, has been listed for $1.485 million (£1.11 million) after being owned by the same family for 80 years. Located at 21 Frontage Road in Blairstown, the property includes a preserved timber-frame barn built in 1839, 21 acres of farmland, and a separate guest cottage. According to local radio station WRNJ, the land is protected by a farmland preservation deed restriction, which means it must remain agricultural land rather than being used for commercial or residential development. According to property details on Realtor.com, the farm is still operating as a choose-and-cut Christmas tree business, alongside active hay fields and open pastures.Historic buildings and living spacesThe main feature of the property is an original English-style Bank Barn built in 1839. The barn still has its original heavy timber frame, traditional mortise-and-tenon joints, and loft space used for storing farm equipment and supplies. The property also includes a main house and a separate guest cottage. Records on Realtor.com show that the cottage has its own kitchen, bathroom, and utilities, giving it an independent living space. It could be used by farm workers, guests, or as a rental. The land includes farmland, working Christmas tree fields, mature wooded areas, and a natural stream that runs through the property.Farmland preservation protects the landThe property's permanent preservation status prevents future owners from dividing the 135 acres into housing developments. Under New Jersey's Farmland Preservation Program, the restrictions stay with the property even when ownership changes. According to the New Jersey Department of Agriculture, preserved farms must continue to be used for agriculture, soil conservation, and open-space protection. The rules allow activities such as timber harvesting, growing crops, and raising livestock, while preventing industrial development. For buyers, the farmland designation can also lead to lower property taxes under local farmland assessment rules.80 years of family ownershipThe current owners bought the Blairstown property 80 years ago and gradually turned parts of the land into a commercial Christmas tree business serving families across northern New Jersey during the holiday season. According to WRNJ, the farm expanded over the middle of the 20th century to include rotating crops and hay production. The sale is the first time in 80 years that the land, buildings, and business rights have been offered on the open market. Listing agents from Coldwell Banker Realty say the property is being sold with existing farm equipment, field infrastructure, and established customer routes for the Christmas tree business.Warren County’s agricultural marketThe listing comes as demand remains steady for preserved farmland in northwestern New Jersey. Warren County has thousands of acres protected through state preservation programs designed to prevent rural areas from being replaced by growing towns and suburbs. Data from the New Jersey State Agriculture Development Committee shows that Warren County has one of the largest amounts of preserved farmland in the state. Local communities also support agritourism businesses such as pick-your-own farms and seasonal Christmas tree operations. Potential buyers have until late autumn to submit offers through the listing brokers. Closing arrangements will be planned around the upcoming holiday tree harvest season.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: California’s 1,921-acre Mead Ranch is now protected as a $24 million acquisition strengthens wildlife corridors around Coyote Valley
articles.summary: US News: A 1,921-acre ranch in California’s Santa Cruz Mountains has become part of a much larger conservation landscape after the Peninsula Open Space Trust a.
articles.body: A 1,921-acre ranch in California’s Santa Cruz Mountains has become part of a much larger conservation landscape after the Peninsula Open Space Trust acquired the property for $24 million in 2026. Mead Ranch, located in Santa Clara County west of Morgan Hill, sits between existing open-space preserves and forms part of a patchwork of roughly 50,000 acres of protected and open land around the South Bay’s Coyote Valley. The acquisition is intended to protect the ranch and its wildlife habitat, while the property could eventually help fill a gap in the Bay Area Ridge Trail, although public access and a trail route have not yet been confirmed.California’s ranch links nearly 50,000 acres of protected landMead Ranch's location is significant because it sits between existing protected areas. According to the San Francisco Chronicle, conservationists have highlighted the landscape as a corridor for animals including mountain lions and bobcats. The wider area also supports species such as the bay checkerspot butterfly, California tiger salamander and western pond turtle, along with other endemic wildlife.Marti Tedesco, POST’s senior manager of media and communications, described the area as important for wildlife. “What we’ve seen is, in fact, this is pretty much one of the most vital linkages,” Tedesco told the San Francisco Chronicle, referring to its importance not only for mountain lions and bobcats but also for other plant and animal species. The conservation group has not announced a detailed management or public-access plan for the property.Mead Ranch could add 1.5 miles to the Bay Area Ridge TrailThe acquisition could also help the Bay Area Ridge Trail, a planned 550-mile loop around the region. Roughly 415 miles of the trail have already been established, while Mead Ranch could eventually provide about 1.5 miles of additional route. The property therefore sits near an existing gap in the developing trail network.However, access and trail construction are not yet confirmed. POST has no firm plan to open Mead Ranch to the public at present, although the organisation believes the property could eventually provide an appropriate connection for the Ridge Trail. POST says it can't discuss a route until it learns where key species and habitats are on the property.California’s Mead Ranch purchase protects 1,921 acres of landFor now, the primary purpose of the acquisition is conservation rather than recreation. POST acquired Mead Ranch specifically to protect its 1,921 acres, making the property part of a much larger landscape of conserved and open-space land around Coyote Valley. The purchase therefore adds another large block to an interconnected conservation area rather than simply creating a standalone preserve.The purchase was announced on 3 March 2026 and represents another step in efforts to preserve connected landscapes in the South Bay. POST is still determining how Mead Ranch might eventually be used, including whether it can help close a gap in the Bay Area Ridge Trail. For now, the 1,921-acre ranch remains set aside for protection within the wider 50,000-acre open-space landscape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump, Iranian president converge on NYC for ‘dramatic’ UN showdown as Tehran faces tight restrictions
articles.summary: President Donald Trump and Masoud Pezeshkian converge on New York City for the U.N. General Assembly amid strict U.S. restrictions on Iran's delegation movements.
articles.body: President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are set to converge on New York City for the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) this week, setting up what former White House officials describe as a "dramatic" diplomatic moment, with Tehran’s delegation effectively "captive" under U.S. restrictions amid heightened Middle East tensions. Pezeshkian, for one, is scheduled to address the assembly on Wednesday, Reuters and Iran's semi-official news agency, Mehr, reported Sunday, with Trump at the rostrum on Tuesday. "The choreography here is going to make for a fairly dramatic moment," Theo Wold, former acting assistant attorney general and White House domestic policy advisor, told Fox News Digital. PUTIN, XI AND IRAN'S PEZESHKIAN DESCEND ON INDIA FOR HIGH-STAKES BRICS SUMMIT AMID ESCALATING GLOBAL TENSIONS "For the Iranians, the limitation is going to be that there's going to be less access to the international press and less ability for them to essentially poke the Trump administration in the eye," Wold added before noting that it is "pretty sensible to allow them to participate in the international forum and to discuss whatever issues they think are pertinent to their regime and then tell them to go home." The high-profile gathering also comes as Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran amid the almost seven-month war. Tehran, meanwhile, has set seven conditions for talks with Washington, according to Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. Iran also warned on Sunday against any big new attack by the United States and its allies, saying it had information such a move was being prepared, Reuters reported. While the U.S. approved visas for Iran’s delegation earlier this week, including Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, the State Department has placed strict limits on Iranian movements while in Manhattan. As the host country under a 1947 U.N. agreement, the United States generally must facilitate the entry and transit of foreign representatives traveling to U.N. headquarters, including officials from adversarial nations. "While ordinary Iranians endure brutal repression, water and electricity shortages, and soaring inflation, the regime's officials want to go on shopping sprees in New York. Not on our watch," U.S. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said on X. UN WATCHDOG SLAMS POTENTIAL ELECTION OF IRAN TO PANEL WITH HUMAN RIGHTS SWAY: 'LUNATICS RUNNING THE ASYLUM' For Washington, Wold said the U.S. is not obligated to give them unrestricted access beyond diplomatic responsibilities. "Here, the delegation will be restricted to their accommodation in New York City and the U.N. headquarters there in Manhattan," Wold clarified. He characterized the move by Washington as a way of telling the delegation it could participate in official discussions but not "go and buy a bunch of microwaves or a small car at Costco or a dealership in the greater New York area." "Some of the restrictions fully recognize that when Iran comes to New York for UNGA, really it's about them lining their pockets and going on shopping sprees to get household appliances and Rolex watches," Wold said. "They're not going to be going on shopping sprees. They're certainly not going to be hitting up Michelin-starred restaurants in greater Manhattan. "They also go to Sam’s Club and Walmart and Costco. And that was one of the specific prohibitions issued by the State Department this week: to contact those big-box retailers that require a basic membership and say, ‘You’re not to transact or do any business with Iranians when they arrive, and you’re to notify us when they do.’" KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL Despite the restrictions, Wold said UNGA gives Washington the opportunity it has "wanted for quite some time to have a large enough audience, and a sort of captive Iranian delegation" to make some of the essential points for why the administration pursued the actions it did against the Iranian regime. Iranian state media also reported Sept. 19 that Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said New York held "absolutely no charm" for the Iranian delegation. Baghaei, Mehr News Agency reported, went on to accuse the U.S. of using every tool to block the delegation’s participation, asserting that Iran’s attendance is a legal right rather than a favor. Wold went on to criticize the U.N. for hosting state representatives hostile to American interests while raising security concerns. "It's going to be one of those things that's fairly perplexing to most Americans," Wold said. "How is it that the representatives of what we have long identified as a hostile regime, but now one that we're actually engaged in combat operations against, one that has killed American service members, why is it that their diplomats get to come to the United Nations and exchange niceties with other kleptocrats or some of their other allies on the international scene?" TWO US SERVICE MEMBERS KILLED IN IRANIAN STRIKES ON JORDAN, CENTCOM SAYS Wold also added that the United Nations wants to "lecture us about international climate change or the need to trans children, but the other is happy to sort of serve as a forum for obvious violators of human rights and obvious regimes that are contrary to any number of internationally agreed-upon protocols." Amid the hostility between Washington and Tehran, Wold said the gathering could also provide an opening for diplomacy. Trump is also slated to hold bilateral and sideline meetings with leaders from the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to discuss regional security and the Strait of Hormuz. "There's the hope that there'll be an opportunity for real discussion," Wold said of UNGA. "Everyone's hope, especially from State Department leadership, is that there'll be an opportunity to have a fulsome, sort of meaningful discussion with the Iranians, freed from some of the theatrics the Iranians have engaged in. Wold expressed confidence in Washington’s posture heading into the summit. "The president is best equipped for these moments. This is really where he sort of shines as a natural leader," he said. "He's not one to bend or to break. It's a precarious time for President Trump, but I have no doubt at all that he'll rise to the moment."

articles.title: Illegal off-roading: Police to seize 4x4s and bikes 'on the spot'
articles.summary: With damage to protected habitats reportedly rising, police have powers to seize illegal off-roading vehicles on the spot.
articles.body:
Police say off-road drivers causing anti-social behaviour or damage to protected habitats will have their vehicles seized "on the spot".

PC Eryl Lloyd, of North Wales Police's rural crime team, said new powers allowed officers to take vehicles without notice, and warned offending drivers: "It's a long walk home."

Both the force and Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said damage caused by off-roading incidents and other anti-social behaviour was on the rise.

In August, three men who caused "irreversible" harm to the Berwyn Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) in 4x4s were convicted after videos of them causing the damage were shared on TikTok.

Off-roaders caught damaging protected site after posting videos to TikTok

John Robinson, Michael Williams and Joseph Hodgson were part of a seven-vehicle convoy which drove from Liverpool to the Berwyn range, an area of moorland in northeast Wales, where they caused "serious damage" to the peat and bog habitat.

Robinson and Williams were fined more than £2,000 each and disqualified from driving for two months. Hodgson was ordered to pay £1,000 compensation for damaging the SSSI, as well as costs, and was also banned from entering the Berwyn SSSI for three years.

PC Eryl Lloyd – who is seconded to NRW – said his team had "definitely seen an increase in off-roading incidents".

As well as 4x4 vehicles and motorbikes, "we're getting a lot more reports about e-bikes, which also cause the same amount of damage as motorbikes" he added.

Under the Crime and Policing Act 2026, introduced earlier this year, police have new powers to tackle the problem.

"Previously, we had to give a warning for incidents of anti-social behaviour, careless driving.

"Now we can just seize the vehicles there on the spot.

"We will use these new powers and we will be seizing vehicles on the spot as well."

Although the reason for a rise in off-roading incidents is unknown, Lloyd believed it was "to do with social media" and people sharing locations.

He added: "They come from all over the UK. We are very close to the northwest of England. But we've seen people travelling from the Midlands, even London as well."

While social media may have contributed to a rise in off-road incidents, Lloyd also said: "We've had incidents over the summer in Newborough Forest, Newborough Beach [Anglesey], where social media has exploded.

"And the amount of people coming to wild-camp, and causing anti-social behaviour from that, from illegal fires to barbecues… so it's been a busy summer."

On the Berwyn Range, damage which led to the convictions of drivers last month included the wearing away of hundreds of years worth of peat growth.

Kirsty Roberts, of NRW, said: "On this specific occasion we're talking about peatlands, which are really slow-growing habitats.

"So in this particular scenario we had a depth of 40cm (15in) worth of peat, which equates to around 400 years worth of peat depth and peat growth.

"And so, to see this area naturally recover, we just wouldn't see it in our lifetime."

Damage caused by off-road vehicles to peatlands and vegetation also impact wildlife, including ground-nesting birds, she said.

Without intervention to avoid further degradation, she warned: "We're not going to be able to reverse that biodiversity curve."

As well as a rise in 4x4 and e-bike incidents, she said "general anti-social behaviour" was also increasing, including use of barbecues and "a lot of waste being dumped on protected sites", adding: "It's happening on areas that are really fragile."

Lord Newborough, of the Rhug Estate in Denbighshire, owns the Berwyn land damaged by the off-roaders convicted last month.

He said areas of the estate had been opened up "for the public to enjoy", but "the mountain is very precious and we've tried to protect that and be good custodians for many years".

He agreed that damage to important habitats caused by off-road vehicles was becoming more frequent.

"I feel gutted basically because this is damage that has happened in recent years."

Under the Countryside and Rights of Way Act, a fifth of Wales is classed as "access land" including areas where land owners have agreed the public have a right of entry on foot.

"I'm pretty old myself, so I grew up respecting the mountains and not seeing the encroachment that we've got by the public now.

"So, yes it hurts me and it hurts, the fact that the damage has been done.

"We monitor the bird life on the mountain every year and we know that certain precious nests are being damaged wilfully, and this isn't really the way ahead."

articles.title: ICE shooting rocks Austin as Democrat demands bodycam video, independent probe
articles.summary: Austin police say a brief foot pursuit involving ICE ended with an adult man shot once in the torso and hospitalized in serious but stable condition.
articles.body: An angry crowd erupted in yelling, whistles and obscenities near the scene of an ICE-involved shooting that left an adult man seriously wounded on an Austin street Sunday. Video from the scene showed people holding up their phones and carrying flags as the commotion unfolded. Police said preliminary information indicated the man was shot once in the torso during a brief foot pursuit involving ICE. He remained hospitalized in serious but stable condition. Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis and Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz confirmed ICE was involved in the shooting and provided what they repeatedly stressed were preliminary details during a Sunday afternoon news conference. Austin-Travis County EMS was notified of the shooting at approximately 12:56 p.m. and arrived in less than five minutes, Luckritz said. The adult man was taken from the scene within nine minutes and transported to a local trauma center in serious but stable condition after being shot once in the torso. Davis said preliminary information indicated there was a brief foot pursuit before the shooting, but cautioned that she had not yet been briefed by federal authorities. 'SQUAD' MEMBER CALLS DHS 'GREATEST THREAT TO OUR SAFETY' AFTER ICE-INVOLVED SHOOTING "From what I'm hearing, there was a small foot pursuit," Davis said. "But again, this is all very preliminary." Watson stressed that the information available was "extremely preliminary." He said city officials wanted to make themselves available as quickly as possible when they had information, but warned against rushing to conclusions based on early claims circulating on TikTok, X and other social media platforms. Watson added that the Austin Police Department was not involved in the shooting and only assisted with traffic control. APD's Special Investigations Unit and the Texas Rangers will work together to investigate the incident, Davis said. "The city of Austin deserves answers," Davis said. "We're going to get all those questions answered, and we'll be as transparent as we can be." Watson said he was "very angry" and "extremely unhappy" about the shooting, while accusing ICE of creating fear and chaos in Austin and other cities. He also questioned the agency's ability to investigate itself without local involvement. ICE AGENTS IN FATAL HOUSTON SHOOTING WERE NOT WEARING BODY CAMERAS, SOURCES SAY Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, claimed in a post on X that "ICE has shot a person in Austin this morning" and called for a full, independent investigation and the immediate release of body-camera footage. "Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened," Casar wrote. "We will demand truth, transparency and accountability." During the news conference, Casar called the incident part of a "disturbing pattern" and said ICE's conduct "has got to stop." "They've arrested 5-year-olds ... and now someone has been shot," Casar said. "This has got to stop." Authorities have not identified the man who was shot or fully disclosed what led to the encounter. The Austin investigation comes amid heightened tensions over federal immigration enforcement operations across the country. ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS CLASH WITH AGENTS OUTSIDE NEW JERSEY DETENTION CENTER AS GOV SHERRILL DENIED ENTRY Clashes erupted outside New Jersey's Delaney Hall immigration detention center in May after protesters defied a state police order to move to a designated demonstration area. Newark Mayor Ras Baraka later criticized the tactics used by state troopers sent to secure the facility, which had become the focus of frequent demonstrations. Federal immigration operations also drew national scrutiny in Minnesota following the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. Good was killed by an ICE agent in early January after authorities said she tried to use her vehicle to run over federal officers, while Pretti was fatally shot by agents on Jan. 24 as he recorded federal officers. articles.title: Vouliagmeni beach: Man, 82, dies after beach fight with 76-year-old over sunlounger in Greece
articles.summary: One eyewitness said the scene was so chaotic that screaming could be heard from the other end of the beach.
articles.body:
An 82-year-old man has died after getting into a fight with a man in his 70s over a sunlounger on a beach in Greece, local media is reporting.

Witnesses say a disagreement over the use of the loungers at Vouliagmeni beach, near Athens, escalated into a violent fight, which then further spiralled to involve other people.

One eyewitness told the Kathimerini newspaper that the scene was so chaotic, the screaming could be heard from the other end of the beach.

The younger man, who was 76, has reportedly been arrested. A 21-year-old woman who was with him was also detained but later released. Witnesses told Ta Nea daily newspaper that she had a bloodied and swollen face.

During the fight, the 82-year-old collapsed. According to various reports, he received CPR and a defibrillator was used on him before an ambulance arrived. The man was taken to hospital where he later died.

Another witness said that the victim seemed to be waiting for other people and had reserved a sunlounger, which appeared to be the cause of the initial disagreement.

Authorities are investigating what led to the physical altercation and what caused the man's death.

articles.title: ICE agent shoots and wounds man in Austin, Texas, officials say
articles.summary: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man Sunday afternoon in Texas' capital of Austin, local authorities said, and anti-ICE...
articles.body:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man Sunday afternoon in Texas' capital of Austin, local authorities said, and anti-ICE protesters quickly gathered at the scene.

The unnamed man was in serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on the city's north side, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said at a news conference with the mayor and other city officials.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not participate in the news conference and didn't immediately respond to requests for details.

Austin police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, which occurred after a traffic stop, Davis told reporters.

Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said he wants the city's police department to be involved in the investigation so it can provide "clear, third-party eyes" in the process. Watson said he does not think it would be appropriate for ICE to conduct an investigation on its own.

Austin residents have "a right to feel safe in their city," Watson said. A proper investigation will only enhance credibility, he added.

Davis said she did not yet know the nationality of the person who was shot. The chief said there were not many facts she could provide so soon after the incident, but added that her department's special investigation unit was at the scene.

A dark blue Toyota Corolla was parked under an overpass with damage to its passenger-side door and what appeared to be bullet holes, local media reported.

A large law enforcement presence was at the scene, along with a crowd of about a hundred protesters. Some demonstrators cursed at police officers holding riot shields, while others yelled out as passing cars honked in support of the protest. One man held a sign saying, "Nobody is safe" and, on the other side, "ICE Nazi."

Asked if Austin authorities knew where the involved federal agent is, given that agents have left states after previous shootings nationwide, the mayor said: "We do not know that. But my hope would be that, an agent that's involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city. Certainly not leave the state."

U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.

"It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," Casar told reporters. "For Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here."

The shooting comes as ICE surges enforcement across the country this summer, producing more than 50,000 arrests a month for the first time in its history in July and August.

In July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, of Houston, after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site.

Also in July, 25-year-old Johan Sebastián, a Colombian man, was shot by an ICE officer in Maine . The officer is an Army veteran who has struggled with serious mental health issues since early childhood and never should have been given a badge and gun to patrol American streets, several of his close relatives told The Associated Press.

The administration's enforcement efforts were widely condemned last winter after the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota.

Weber reported from Los Angeles. Contributing were Associated Press journalists Rebecca Boone in Boise, Idaho; Kimberlee Kruesi in Providence, R.I.; and Tim Sullivan in Minneapolis.

articles.title: In 2021, Queen Elizabeth began a tree-planting initiative. By 2023, it became a nationwide memorial with three million trees
articles.summary: UK News: In 2021, Queen Elizabeth II joined the then Prince of Wales to launch a tree-planting initiative that would continue beyond the Platinum Jubilee itsel.
articles.body: In 2021, Queen Elizabeth II joined the then Prince of Wales to launch a tree-planting initiative that would continue beyond the Platinum Jubilee itself. The idea was straightforward: people across the United Kingdom could plant trees as part of a nationwide tribute to the Queen’s 70 years on the throne. What began as a Jubilee project eventually took on a second purpose in September 2022. Planting was extended into the following spring, allowing trees to be added in her memory. By the time the Queen’s Green Canopy came to an end in March 2023, more than three million trees had been planted across the UK, leaving behind a physical record of a national celebration.Queen Elizabeth II launched the tree-planting project in 2021The Queen’s Green Canopy was created around Queen Elizabeth II’s Platinum Jubilee in 2022. Its central invitation was for individuals, communities, schools, organisations and others to take part by planting trees.As reported by official The Royal Family UK, the Queen and the then Prince of Wales launched the initiative by planting a tree in the grounds of Windsor Castle. The first tree planting season officially began in October 2021, marked by a further planting at the Balmoral Estate with local schoolchildren, before activity spread to locations around the country.The scheme was not limited to large estates or official ceremonies. Trees could be planted by people and organisations in many different settings, with the wider aim of building a lasting record of the Jubilee rather than concentrating the planting in one location.70 ancient trees and 70 ancient woodlands were highlightedAlongside the new planting, the initiative drew attention to trees and woodlands that were already part of the UK landscape.Reportedly, 70 ancient woodlands and 70 ancient trees were highlighted during the Jubilee period. The selection connected the new planting programme with older parts of the landscape, including trees and woodland that had survived for generations.That distinction mattered to the project because the QGC was not simply about adding new trees. It also provided a way to recognise established natural features while marking an important point in the Queen’s reign.Hundreds of young trees came together for the Jubilee’s “Tree of Trees”The planting programme also featured a large temporary installation created for the Platinum Jubilee celebrations in London.Known as the QGC “Tree of Trees”, the structure was made from hundreds of young native trees arranged around a central framework. The trees represented the many plantings taking place across the country and gave the nationwide project a physical presence during the Jubilee celebrations.After the event, the individual trees were made available for planting at locations around the UK. The installation therefore became another link between the Jubilee celebrations and the longer-term planting programme.Queen Elizabeth II’s death gave the final planting season a new purposeQueen Elizabeth II died in September 2022, several months after the Platinum Jubilee celebrations. The planting initiative could have ended with the Jubilee year, but it was extended following a request from its patron, now King Charles III.The additional planting season ran until March 2023. This gave people another opportunity to plant trees in remembrance of the Queen, changing the character of the final months of the project. Trees planted during this period therefore carried two connected associations: the celebration of the Queen’s 70-year reign and remembrance following her death.More than three million trees were eventually plantedAcross its two planting seasons, the Queen’s Green Canopy recorded more than three million trees planted throughout the United Kingdom. The scale of the final figure reflected participation from a wide range of communities and organisations rather than a single planting operation. The trees were also recorded through an interactive QGC map, allowing the locations associated with the initiative to be represented geographically.By March 2023, the planting phase had finished. What remained was a distributed collection of trees in places across the UK, rather than one single memorial site.A living record of the JubileeThe Queen’s Green Canopy was unusual in that its final legacy was spread across the country. A tree planted for the project could stand in a community space, woodland, garden, school grounds or another suitable location, with each contributing to the wider record.The more than three million trees therefore represent the combined planting activity of the initiative's two seasons. The project began as a way to mark a royal milestone in 2022, was extended after Queen Elizabeth’s death, and finished in 2023 with the planting programme transformed into a lasting memorial as well as a Jubilee legacy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
